summary: The blog used Lunr.js, a Lucene/Solr-inspired full-text search library in JavaScript, running in the user's browser against a searchable index of the site's content. For typeahead, it runs a search after each keystroke (once at least two characters are typed), combining exact term matches with a higher boost and trailing-wildcard prefix matches with a lower boost.

In the text-to-speech script, pydub is used to stitch the temporary MP3 chunks returned by the API into one completed file, which is then written to a suitable directory before cleaning up the chunks. The passages describe it as an audio-handling library the blog has used before.
The blog does not seem to cover this. None of the provided passages mention the mmh3 library.

The blog's examples use the mmh3 library to hash elements, with the number of hash functions used as the seed so each hash function produces a different result. The remainder of each hash divided by the bit array size then gives the index to set (for example, in its m=15, k=3 example, the string "hello" sets bits at indices 1, 7 and 10).

Make sure your OpenSearch XML file is available from your webserver, then refresh the page containing the link so browsers can discover it, as the blog describes. This works when your site's search is accessible through a basic GET request, and some browsers need a more formalized configuration instead of autodiscovery.

TF-IDF ranking multiplies each matching term's frequency in a document by its inverse document frequency, computed as the logarithm of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents containing that term, so rare terms contribute more to the relevancy score. The blog's passages describe this, along with the index-based lookup and the fact that it only matches the same words used in documents.

Passage [1] says sentence-transformers is free because it runs locally, while OpenAI's embeddings endpoint is a hosted API, so the main tradeoff is cost and local execution versus a hosted service. The passages don't go into further detail on why one would be preferred over the other.

The passages do not explain why the blog switched to PaperMod; they only note that PaperMod was the most popular Hugo theme according to the analysis, and that the commit "Add PaperMod theme and convert config to YAML" was made. The blog does not seem to cover the specific reasoning behind that choice.

The local coding agent runs Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, a 4-bit mixture-of-experts model with about 30B total parameters and roughly 3B active per token. The blog's recommended setup later swaps the serving layer to LM Studio, but the model stays the same.

Semantic search finds documents by meaning rather than exact word matches, bridging the vocabulary gap between how you phrase a query and how the document is written. The blog's post "Building a semantic search engine in ±250 lines of Python" covers this approach, with the examples "Alcoholic beverage disaster" finding beer poisoning articles and "Large constricting reptiles"

A Bloom filter is a memory-cheap way to test set membership when occasional wrong answers are acceptable, since it can return false positives but never false negatives. The blog notes you can tune how rare false positives are by sizing the bit array and choosing the number of hash functions based on the expected number of elements.

The blog's Python full-text search post shows the approach: use an inverted index to find candidate document IDs for each query token, then score each matching document by relevance (the simple method is counting how often the query terms appear in it) and sort by that score. The passages don't go into further detail on how the scoring or indexing achieves millisecond response times at that scale.

You can use Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, a deep learning text-to-speech model, to create an audio version of your blog posts and host it on your website. The passages describe converting the text into chunks, configuring a voice (such as es-US-Wavenet-B), and writing out MP3 files.

The blog suggests using Let's Encrypt, where a certificate management agent proves control of your domain by completing a challenge (such as provisioning a DNS record or serving a file at a specific URL) and then requests, renews, and revokes certificates. It also notes that on GitHub Pages you can enforce HTTPS in the repository settings, and that using A records may require updating your DN

The passages don't describe an AI assistant being asked to overhaul an old website setup. The blog does mention Claude helping with the Kokoro text-to-speech pipeline setup, but that is not a website overhaul, so the blog does not seem to cover that.

The blog suggests running a local coding agent as a fallback for when your budget runs out. Specifically, it describes pairing the Pi agent with a local server running the 4-bit Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B model (about 17 GB of weights), and notes that Claude Code and Codex can also be pointed at a local server, though they reintroduce prompt-caching

The passages describe CrawlerVerse, a roguelike dungeon crawler with an API designed for AI agents, where an agent receives observations each turn (visible tiles, monsters, items, inventory, stats) and chooses actions like move, attack, wait, or pickup. They don't explain how to build such an agent in detail, beyond noting that you call run_game with a model_id

The passages say the original Wikipedia data source was discontinued, and the modernized project now uses Hugging Face (🤗) datasets as its data source. The passages describe the switch to Hugging Face datasets but do not name the specific Wikipedia dataset that replaced the discontinued one.

Visitors can search your site from the address bar by enabling OpenSearch: your site needs a search page that handles an HTTP GET request, an OpenSearch XML file describing it (with a `{searchTerms}` template), and a `<link>` in the page head so browsers can autodiscover the search engine. Some browsers pick this up automatically, while others need the OpenSearch X

According to the blog, there are three options: use a third-party service like Google Custom Search Engine, run a server-side search engine backend, or search client-side. The passages describe the trade-offs of each but do not give step-by-step instructions for implementing any of them.

The blog has written about building a full-text search engine in about 150 lines of Python, using about 6.27 million English Wikipedia abstracts as data, with code available on GitHub. It has also covered a semantic search engine written in roughly 250 lines of Python that can match concepts like "alcoholic beverage disaster" to a post titled "London Beer Flood."

The blog explains that GitHub Pages with a custom domain gets free SSL automatically via Let's Encrypt, which works behind the scenes once you set up a CNAME file for your domain. You can then optionally enforce HTTPS in your repository settings so HTTP visitors are redirected to HTTPS.

The blog describes running a local coding agent built from the Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B model and the minimal Pi agent, and it argues that speed alone doesn't show whether the model writes correct code, so it built a small pytest-based eval. It also covers using Claude Code to migrate an outdated Hugo blog by having the LLM produce a migration plan.

The passages describe generating the index with Hugo Output Formats by adding a JSON output for the homepage (index.json) in config.toml, which the blog says serves as the search index. They also mention running a Grunt task (`grunt search-index`) to produce a JSON index file, but they don't explain how to run that step automatically during the Hugo build.

The blog explains that a Bloom filter uses a bit array of m bits (e.g., 15) and k hash functions, where each element is hashed (using mmh3 with the hash index as a seed) and the remainder modulo the array size selects the bit positions to set to 1. You can create an audio version of a blog post by using a text-to-speech service, such as Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, to convert the post's text into audio files and then embedding them in the post with an audio player shortcode. The author also describes a Python script that parses the Markdown, splits it into chunks under the API's size limit, converts each chunk to MP3, and stitches them together

The blog explains that embeddings are vectors learned from large amounts of text, where similar meanings end up near each other in the vector space (e.g., "king" and "queen" are close, "king" and "bicycle" are far apart). For cosine similarity, it only notes that it is the standard measure for judging how close two vectors are in the embedding space, without going into the formula.

The blog mentions that the author's Hugo blog ran on a 2018 theme called hyde-x, and that they migrated to a modern Hugo theme with Claude Code while preserving URLs and custom features like an audio player shortcode, a bloom filter visualization, and custom CSS for code blocks and figures. It does not go into detail about how to customize a Hugo theme

The blog describes running Kokoro, an 82-million-parameter open-weight text-to-speech model, locally on an M1 MacBook Air with no cloud dependency. It also mentions that the post on memory-mapped files helps a laptop handle large matrices, but the passages don't discuss running language models on your own hardware specifically.
